IN bottom-line terms, Relational Child Psychotherapy is an important, very worthwhile book. As an introductory text for graduate and postdoctoral students interested in a more “current” view of psychodynamic child treatment, it is a worthy addition to, and in some respects an extension beyond, similar recent endeavors by Chethik (1989) and Siskind (1999). At the same time, however, there is a tone throughout the work, but most especially in its last, integrating chapters, that creates an unnecessary “straw man” argument that significantly lessens its appeal. Indeed, the authors' need to extol the virtues of the “relational” approach in contrast to “classical psychoanalysis” renders the former an “all good,” integrative tour de force, while reducing the latter to an anachronistic relic of a pre-World War II zeitgeist. This would have stronger credence if the authors did a much better job of acknowledging how their approach rests on the shoulders of the Freuds (father and daughter) and Klein, instead of largely depicting their limitations.

But let us first return to the virtues of the book, as there are many.

Frank Summers PHD ABPP

Frank Summers

333 East Ontario, Suite 4509B

Frank Summers  

HISTORICALLY, psychoanalysis has addressed time primarily from the perspective of the past. Such a temporal focus was perhaps inevitable given that the psychoanalytic theory of pathogenesis has always emphasized early experience, whether the childhood roots of pathology are conceived as actual events or early fantasy life. By no means does the present article call into question the notion that the patient's early experience is a crucial dimension of the analytic enterprise. It is, however, the thesis here that a temporal orientation focused almost exclusively on the past has limited both the analyst's understanding of the patient and the ability of the analyst to help the patient transcend the quandaries of the past.

The most notable exception to the temporal focus on the past from the classical perspective has been the theoretical work of Hans Loewald. Using ego-psychological language, Loewald (1962) pointed out that the expectations, demands, and prohibitions that become organized into the superego determine the psyche's relationship to the future. Thus, from Loewald's viewpoint, the concept of the superego brings the future into the psychological organization. In a later contribution, Loewald (1972) showed that the objective measure of time as a linearity consisting of past-present-future is not adequate for psychoanalysis, because time is experienced as an interaction of the three temporal modes, rather than a linearity. Despite his recognition that motives can be either forced from the past or attracted by the future, however, Loewald continued the psychoanalytic lineage of looking at the future primarily as affected by the past, while minimizing the influence of the future on the experience of past and present. Although Loewald understood theoretically that temporal experience is an interaction among the three temporal modes, he continued to consider the future primarily as a product of past influence, while giving little attention to the impact of future experience on the construction of past and present.

THIS is a difficult topic for psychoanalysts. For one thing, most of us are not trained to think about larger social systems, such as organizations, much less professions. As Marylou Lionells notes, it is easy to feel unsure of our intellectual footing in this area. For another, we are in the midst of the topic we are trying to think about. This is always difficult, as we know from our clinical work; but it is doubly difficult in this case because there has been so much mystification in the discussions we have had on the topic of our professional identity—and so much anxiety.

The discussants of my paper make it clear that they are by no means complacent defenders of the status quo. I am deeply heartened by their thoughtful responses, not only to my paper, but also to the many troubling issues we face collectively as psychoanalysts. I have the sense that more and more individuals are engaging this urgent task of probing our professional shortcomings and failures. All the more, then, do I appreciate this opportunity to try again to clarify the issue of professionalization. The comments here have helped me to understand the difficulty of communicating my point about psychoanalysis as a profession.

Like Marylou Lionells, I do not believe that psychoanalysis is dead or dying—but she and I both understand that this “psychoanalysis” is not a set of procedures that involve three, four, or five times weekly visits to a couch. If one thinks of “psychoanalysis” more broadly as an overlapping set of ideas, assumptions, and procedures—what Auden in his elegy for Freud called “a climate of opinion”—it is still lively and still growing. But to look at psychoanalysis this way is to look, for the most part, outside our professional training institutes and associations. Inside those institutions, psychoanalysis is besieged and constricting. The marketing survey commissioned by the American Psychoanalytic Association, to which both Lionells and Meyers refer, is a vivid demonstration of that, as is the dilemma of the shrinking pool of talented applicants for training that Newirth refers to in his comments. It is that discrepancy—between our organization as a profession and the vitality of psychoanalysis as a set of ideas and practices—that has animated me to pursue this issue.

NANCY CHODOROW is a distinct voice in psychoanalytic thinking. As a feminist, sociologist, and psychoanalytic theorist, she has in recent decades brought her searching mind and postmodernist sensibility to reconsider a range of issues where the social, cultural, and psychological intersect, including sexism, gender relations, and homophobia. In The Power of Feelings, she elaborates and revises her views on an array of intellectual and theoretical concerns.

The book, a scholarly and forcefully presented work of broad scope and complexity, is a contemporary “contribution to our understanding of individual subjectivity” (p. 1), rooted in psychoanalytic clinical concepts, with emphasis on the transference. Chodorow returns to the central theme of the relationship between psyche and culture, in theory, human experience, and in the clinical encounter. Opposed to simplistic, either-or conceptual approaches within academic and psychoanalytic thought that emphasize either external social and cultural determinants, or inner determinants exclusively, she advocates viewing psyche and culture as an intertwined and coconstructing process. In the mind, she asserts, the cultural and the personal are inextricable.

At the core of Chodorow's thesis, and at odds with contemporary contructivist trends, is her affirmation of the role unconscious psychological life plays in mediating the area “in-between” inner and outer reality, ego, and reality, the personal and the cultural. Her goal is to demonstrate the interpretative power of psychoanalytic discoveries, and clinical processes in particular, for an understanding of this interrelationship. She elaborates a theory of personal meaning, arguing for a view of emergent subjectivity actively shaped by both external (the sociocultural and historical) and internal (psychodynamic and psychobiographical) sources of experience (p. 2).

Lallene Rector  

IN HER BOOK, Rochelle Kainer proposes a number of connections between Melanie Klein' object relations theory and Heinz Kohut' psychology of the self. The attempt to bring two such theories together

162

in ways that will enhance both seems at first a dubious proposition, at least at the theoretical level. What two theorists could have more opposed and contradictory views of human nature than Klein and Kohut? And yet, Kainer offers the reader a creative clinical integration that she both embodies and illustrates to good effect.

The book is divided into three major sections: “Creating the Self,” “The Collapse of the Self,” and “The Therapeutic Restoration of the Self.” Throughout the volume concepts of self, identification, narcissistic injury, object, schizoid-paranoid and depressive positions, psychic structure, imagination, projective identification, empathy, and self object emerge in relation to each other. Kainer explicitly develops links between Klein and Kohut by suggesting (1) containment as a selfobject function, (2) “imaginative empathy” as a dimension of projective identification, (3) that narcissistic injuries precede or precipitate a collapse of the self into the paranoid-schizoid position (with rage as a common affect), and (4) that the paranoid-schizoid and depressive positions have experience-near “state-of-being” dimensions in a given moment.

Kainer focuses on the central role of identification(s) in the formation and structure of the self. Following a comprehensive literature review, she addresses two broad types of identification, ideal and pathological, suggesting a dialectical tension between them. This dialectic and the particular balance in the personality of ideal and pathological identifications help to determine the nature of the patient' life narrative as well as the analytic experience. The task of treatment then becomes the transformation of pathological identifications and assisting the patient in the acceptance of all parts of the self.

Identification with an ideal object represents a will toward self-creation and becomes the ideal self to be fulfilled. These identifications have a “transcendent” force and constitute a part of the self that is “non-psychotic, non-autistic, enduring, connected, playful, thoughtful, resilient, and creative” (p. 37). A chapter devoted to the role of identification in art illustrates Kainer' creativity in thought and practice throughout the volume. She argues that art has a projective pull originating from the source of the ideal object, the lost object, and the ideal self. In an unusual piece of analytic writing, Kainer offers a self-analysis of her response to a Japanese novel, The Makioka Sisters (Junichiro Tanizaki, 1943-48) and its relation to her own ideals for psychoanalysis.

ARGUABLY, the psychoanalytic world in Germany in the 1920s and early 1930s was the most fertile, imaginative, collegial, and creative psychoanalytic community our profession has ever known. Although psychoanalysis was born in Vienna, nourished through its early years almost single-handedly by Freud and the small group of loyalist collaborators who met with him there, it was in Germany that our field blossomed as it never had in Austria.

Known for his consummate organizational skill, Karl Abraham was a member of Freud's once-secret “Committee” and (until his death in 1925) headed Berlin's psychoanalytic institute, widely regarded as the ideal model of institutional organization and functioning. Its training model—tripartite functions of course work, personal analysis, and supervised “control analysis”—embodied what remains today the prevailing model world-wide (Kernberg, 2000) of institutional training in psychoanalysis.

History continues to exhume and record the extraordinary events associated with the rise of National Socialism in Germany. In this context, pointed questions have been raised about the fate of psychoanalysis in the years concurrent with Hitler's rise to power and his drive toward world domination. The data of this record began to amass in the latter decades of the twentieth century, as the world emerged from the numbing effects of wartime events on collective memory and on soul and psyche. James E. Goggin and Eileen Brockman Goggin, two clinical psychologists who practice in Lubbock, Texas, have contributed a remarkable volume to the historical record.

Foreword

Jay Greenberg PHD

Jay Greenberg

275 Central Park West, Apartment 1BB
New York, NY 10024

Jay Greenberg  

STEVE MITCHELL graduated from the William Alanson White Institute in 1977, a year before I did. We had met some six years before that, when we were members of a psychotherapy supervision group in graduate school at New York University.

From the beginning, Steve and I shared a passionate interest in psychoanalysis that was a central part of what quickly became a deep friendship. In addition to family get-togethers, we would meet frequently in the same Chinese restaurant (we had to switch every several years as our favorites went out of business) and, after lengthy deliberation and without really noticing, always order the same dishes. Our conversations wound through the expectable topics but always, eventually, circled back to psychoanalysis. Interested in theory as well as clinical practice, and sharing the training experiences at New York University and White with their inclusive, pluralistic approaches, we were both trying to figure out for ourselves how different conceptual approaches fit together—how they overlapped and where they diverged from each other.

In retrospect, I realize that the conversations Steve and I were having were unusual for the time. For one thing, in keeping with what we had learned in the course of our training, when we talked about “psychoanalysis” we spoke in the same breath of Freud and the ego psychologists and Sullivan and Fairbairn. For another, we assumed that we were psychoanalysts, despite being psychologists and despite not having been trained at an institute of the American Psychoanalytic Association. Of course, we were aware—with a mixture of self-doubt and pride that I remember mostly as a wordless experience—that our claims to professional status wouldn't be accepted by the most orthodox analysts. But those analysts seemed so distant to us that what they thought didn't seem to matter much. For the most part, we were untouched by our exclusion.

Even for me, having lived the history with Steve, it is difficult to grasp how much has changed in what, despite evidence to the contrary, seems like a very short time. Two stories capture what things were like at the beginning of our professional lives.

John O'Leary  

Dr. CARL GOLDBERG'S BOOK is as much a critique of the theory and practice of psychoanalysis as it is a treatise on destructiveness. Dr. Goldberg cannot explain the effectiveness of his therapeutic strategies without showing us how he had to abandon traditional metapsychology in order to do so. The psychoanalysis he attacks is orthodox analysis, and he does it by lambasting Freud for not including the development of a social conscience as an integral part of the human psyche. Freud's notion of the superego is hardly up to the task that Goldberg sees as necessary. Focusing on that part of Freud's theory, which elaborates the superego as the heir to castration anxiety, Goldberg sees its functioning as tied to fears of retaliation. Conscience, on the other hand, ought to have a more compassionate, altruistic character. In fact, “Freud confused conscience and superego” (p. 48).

Goldberg runs some risk of preaching to the converted. To his credit, he does not go after the “usual suspects” in his reproach, such as the detached analyst. Rather, he takes on classical analysis at a more trenchant level, one that requires the reader to look at moral and social considerations. Disciples of Fromm will welcome his critique. Goldberg's reading of classical psychoanalysis is that it portrays human beings as devoid of prosocial motivation and pays excessive attention to interior concerns. The idea that we live in a world with responsibilities towards others is not sufficiently articulated. Analysts working within this framework cannot make compelling appeals for equity, empathy, and repentance because these are seen as defenses. Instead, the analyst must remain neutral even in the face of what Goldberg calls “destructiveness.”

“Destructiveness” is an omnibus word for Goldberg. He uses it as an overarching term for those who act without a conscience—on a spectrum from lying, cheating and minor dishonesty to large-scale crimes such as rape and murder.

Jon Meyer MD

Jon Meyer

2210 Dalewood Road
Baltimore, MD 21093

Jon Meyer  

I DO NOT REMEMBER psychoanalysis in its 1950s heyday. But I grew up professionally in the 1960s and 1970s, when psychoanalysis had the credibility, privileged status, and self-regulation that marked, in Eisold's terms, a successful professionalization “project.” Psychoanalysis was in the public eye and in demand, with waiting lists of patients and candidates. It was a prestigious calling, although even then somewhat outside the intellectual and collegial frame of what might reasonably be considered allies. We have fallen from that state of grace, as it were, and Eisold asks “why”? He also asks how we might return, not to the same place, but to a better one.

There is no doubt that psychoanalysis has its problems. Some are in the broad cultural context of healthcare industrialization. That context includes managed care deprofessionalization of mental health; so-called providers; lowest common denominator, manualized methods; neglecting mind for brain; and mechanistic, descriptive formulations of sentient, dynamic human beings. Dr. Eisold does not examine the effects of this cultural shift, but that is not his focus. While we are not responsible for the profit-cost-driven challenges of “industrialization,” we are responsible for ineffective responses. The failure to mount timely and effective responses is consistent with Eisold's thesis.

He suggests that we look in the mirror for the cause of many, if not most, of our difficulties. He reflects the well-known comment of Pogo, my favorite comic strip sage, who said, “We have met the enemy and he is us.” As Eisold notes, psychoanalytic proactivity and responsivity have been troubled from the beginning by conflicts, theoretical splits, and personal rancor. He suggests that psychoanalysts managed to appear cohesive and obtain a culturally privileged position only through appeal to the authority of Freud, theoretical purity in emulation of Freud, and an emphasis on Freud's pure gold of psychoanalysis. That strategy, however, could only be effective for so long, and its time has run out.

185 East 85th Street

Arthur Feiner  

ONE AFTERNOON, some months ago, I suggested to one patient that between sessions she try to write down her thoughts and feelings, especially in relation to changes that she observed about herself. This degree of direction was unusual for me because I rarely tell a patient to do anything except talk about feelings. I had been working on a book on self-definition and it seemed like a useful way to get a patient to define her own experience (Feiner, 2000). I chose this patient because, after many years of “successful” analysis, she claimed it was now becoming too laborious to express things, that she had not the words nor the clarity, and that the effort itself felt overwhelming.

I introduced the idea as a sort of autobiographical psychoanalytic log (in fact, I called it that, rather than a diary) and I wondered if she thought it might be helpful. She hesitated, saying reluctantly that she'd give it a try, but didn't think much of it or the possibility that it would be useful for her. She commented drearily, with her usual caution and tentativeness, tinted by shades of hopelessness, that she really had nothing to say. I had heard of some therapists using logs or diaries, but had never used the technique myself. I thought that she possibly could express herself better privately if the anxiety of immediate disapproval was lessened.

The depressive triad, including feelings of hopelessness and helplessness, psychomotor retardation, and tautological expressiveness (Spiegel, personal communication, circa 1962), seemed to have recurred despite my incautious presumption that this part of her struggle had been worked through in therapy. My current or ongoing response to all these feelings—which she had expressed many times before—was the same as usual: that is, she was saying something, expressing her feeling, and we could usefully talk about that. The inquiry included something like, Who was the “I” that said “I have nothing to say”? What was she feeling when she said it? What was in her mind?

Jay Greenberg  

THE ESSAYS included in this memorial volume offer their readers a kind of whirlwind tour through some of the most important currents in contemporary American psychoanalysis. Organized around the broad theme of the impact that relational thinking has had on various traditions within and closely adjacent to psychoanalysis, they also address the history of reciprocal influence among the relational model and other models. This process of mutual influence has been decisive in shaping the conceptual landscape within which all analysts operate today.

In this Afterword I record a set of more or less unsystematic reflections that have been inspired by the papers. Reading them has been both illuminating and personally moving for me: illuminating because of the sophistication with which they engage some of the most interesting issues that analysts are thinking about, moving because each paper has reminded me of conversations that Steve Mitchell and I had over the decades of our friendship. Accordingly, the points on which I have commented are those which struck me as most evocative for any one of a variety of reasons; they are not necessarily those the authors themselves would consider central. My musings are intended as the commentary of somebody who lived through the origins and early development of relational psychoanalysis, looking at what has emerged from those early days as reflected in the work of the authors who have generously contributed to this memorial.

Some of what I say returns me to ideas that Steve and I were trying to get at when we wrote Object Relations in Psychoanalytic Theory as an exercise in comparative psychoanalysis (Greenberg & Mitchell, 1983). Others reflect things we talked about when we were rethinking some of the fundamental premises of psychoanalysis through the lens of what we had learned in training outside of what was then the mainstream. All that I discuss reflects a perspective of my own that was first formed in dialogue with Steve over the years.

I AM NOT EXACTLY an unbiased discussant of Dr. Seward's essay. I was one of her supervisors during her analytic training (though I did not supervize her with the patient she presents here). In this paper she makes herself very vulnerable with her patient and with her reading audience, just as she did in supervision. I remember her as among the most honest, open, dedicated, and self-reflective analytic candidates with whom I have had the pleasure to work. In this context, I am invited to discuss this powerful essay perhaps because she has made herself so vulnerable in presenting the material. This is her first analytic training case, she had little experience as a psychotherapist, and was in the process of struggling to effect a transition from being one kind of a doctor to another very different kind of a doctor. She exposes her work with a man who benefited considerably from their relationship, seemingly paradoxically, in part because of the many “errors” she believes she made along the way. Most of us would not be as intrepid: verbatim transcripts that display being seduced in the context of a highly sexualized male-female relationship, decisions about physical boundary that run counter to the psychoanalytic norm, and open expressions of countertransference anger and outrage. The good news is that her patient grew as a person, Dr. Seward expanded as an analyst, and we readers once again have the opportunity to learn that productive analytic work, like any important relationship in life, never proceeds smoothly. THE INTERSECTING import of these two cartoons may, I think, show us some interesting things about creativity and power at this particular moment in Western culture through the unique lens that women's experience gives us. Careful attention to understanding women as they interface with the dual phenomena of creativity and power may offer us something I believe we urgently need: something that extends beyond gender to help us grasp important aspects of our larger world and a cultural transition we're facing right now. It is a transition with all kinds of promise, but one that—and this brings us to the second cartoon—will require some careful consideration if we are to know what's hit us.

One way to sum up our current transition might be to suggest that two crucial insights psychoanalysis came up with at its inception are starting radically to penetrate the way our larger world is looking at all kinds of things. Those things range from the ways we are starting to understand the nature of material reality to the nature of consciousness and the nature of healing. They range from the worlds of physics to philosophy. Ultimately, I think they are going to amount to what is popularly referred to as “a paradigm shift.” And ultimately, I think they stand to alter our views of power and creativity in ways that may be illuminated by looking to women and the ways women experience living in our culture.

The two insights psychoanalysis gave us hinge on acknowledging the power of love and the power of the unconscious. Psychoanalysis got us thinking about the power of both to create and ultimately transform our experience of being in the world.

The Sculpture and the Dust

Michael Civin PHD

Michael Civin

46, Sea Cliff Avenue
Sea Cliff, NY 11579

Michael Civin  

EARLY MORNING SUNLIGHT streaming though the casement windows illuminates tiny flecks of dust that float suspended in the air of my consulting room. The particles glisten and dance before diffusing. In the dust, the stony, chiseled face of the man who never laughs nor cries as he sits across from me, transforms into a baffling, fluid silhouette that undulates behind a sepia of sparkling sea-foam. I imagine that it must always be here, this magical dust from the seashore of endless worlds, but on many other days the dramatic structure of that ever-emotionless face on the other side of the room is so clear and so poignant that I am tricked into feeling that I know not only who shares the room with me, but also who I am as agent of that sharing.

I suspect that most of you who read what I have to say, especially those among you who are analysts, share with me a special pride in the sculptures that you and your patients fashion over the countless sittings that comprise a psychoanalytic treatment; after all, for over a century now we psychoanalysts have chiseled and sanded the words of our theories into a stone-solid likeness of the human psyche, an icon crafted of insight and interpretation, a sculpture carved in meaning, knowing, and understanding that we have turned, smoothed, and polished with such care that we see in it only the singular image of our conscious reflections. Leaning forward in our analysts' chairs, fist against furrowed brow, elbow gouging into knee, we have cast ourselves as the ever-vigilant champions of thought, masters of the art of transforming unconscious into conscious and of reintegrating the dissociated. Scattered around us on the workbench, dozens of tools for our craft sit, readied for use at any minute: dream interpretation, genetic archeology, analysis of free association, of transference and countertransference, of parapraxes and derivatives, of resistance and defense, of identification and projective identification, of the here and now and the then and there. These are tools, words with which we form our words, which we imbue with the power to create meaning and to cast in stone in that meaning, the image of the human being.

Two Faces of Monotheism

Robert Karen PHD

Robert Karen

417 Riverside Drive
New York, NY 10025

Robert Karen  

ONE WEEK after September 11, National Public Radio broadcast a strained and solemn interview with three clergymen concerning their religion's response to terrorism that ended on the subject of forgiveness. The three men all favored it (“Christ forgave those who crucified him …”), the Muslim alone holding out for the necessity of punishment, but none expressing his own hatred of the terrorists or their wishes for revenge. We are accustomed to such bland acts of dissociation when the subject of forgiveness comes up and usually take no notice (“That's just what clergymen do”). But dissociation like this does harm to nuanced discourse, creating an apparent split between muscular realism and ineffectual do-goodism. It is not unrelated to the dissociations, splitting, and quest for purity that we associate with the mind-set of the terrorist.

Terrorists do it differently, of course. They dissociate from their human concern rather than their rage, which enables them to do terrible things to those they perceive as enemies (Segal, 2003). They also view the world as split into good and evil, which entitles them to a hatred and aggression undiluted by doubt. Their passion and certainty, their woundedness and fixation on righteous revenge, can be contagious among people who experience themselves as downtrodden. The pious ideal of forgiveness, in contrast, has very little appeal to anyone, especially in times of strife, and is quietly dismissed as preachy and irrelevant. Bland compassion and piety are no match for paranoia and revenge, which are hard to beat in the best of circumstances. It's rare that a leader like Gandhi emerges who can even temporarily turn this equation into something else.

Because forgiveness is almost always conceptualized in tame and pious terms, its fate since September 11 has not been a happy one: to be spoken about in platitudes and tossed aside as wholly irrelevant to the sort of person one actually is, or to life as one actually lives it. And yet, the subject “Can we forgive?” does keep popping up in public discourse, as if there is an itch in the body politic that needs a scratch. I think the itch is important, but the conceptualization is usually wrong.

Joseph Newirth  

I AM EXTREMELY GRATEFUL to Kenneth Eisold for his important paper. It provides a point of departure for a long-overdue discussion of serious problems in psychoanalysis, including our training programs, our lack of an exciting intellectual focus, and our inability to inspire an informed public. I am in complete agreement with Dr. Eisold's observations and conclusions about the problems and failures in the profession of psychoanalysis, and I would like to elaborate on some of his points, as well as to develop some ideas on possible directions to take in addressing these problems in psychoanalysis.

Eisold begins his discussion from a sociological and organizational perspective, describing the professionalization of psychoanalysis and how it has led to the development of conservative institutions that are more interested in protecting parochial theoretical systems, limited economic interests, and prerogatives of a psychoanalytic oligarchy rather then engaging in a public discourse that would extend the values and knowledge of psychoanalysis. He points out the radical nature of the early psychoanalytic enterprise, which he illustrates with Freud's stand against the sexual hypocrisy of his time and which could also include many other psychoanalytic pioneers. Psychoanalysis as a radical critique of society was central to other seminal thinkers, including Sullivan, Fromm, Horney, Klein, and Lacan. This radical critique of society of early psychoanalysis was at the core of a wider intellectual interest in psychoanalysis as well as its attraction to idealistic and politically conscious individuals who became future psychoanalysts.

Unfortunately, psychoanalysis's radical critique of society has turned inward, becoming a conservative or reactionary critique of nonconforming psychoanalytic institutes and practices. It has devolved to a “paranoid cast to the organizational world of psychoanalysis.

IN 1991 emerged the first issue of Psychoanalytic Dialogues, the journal that Stephen Mitchell had conceived and founded to give expression to relational perspectives at a time when they constituted “if not voices in the wilderness, certainly nonmainstream viewpoints” (Mitchell, 1996, p. 1). On the occasion of its fifth anniversary, by which time classical Freudian theory's hegemony was over and it was relational thinking that was beginning to resemble a new mainstream, Mitchell expressed an anxiety and a challenge: “It is most important that this vitalizing conceptual framework [of relational thinking] be neither degraded into a monolithic model with a set of technical formulas, nor thinned out into a shallow environmentalism.” His recommendation resembled a return to the repressed: “In terms of theory, there is a need for relational authors to address more directly those domains of experience with which classical Freudian theory was most centrally concerned: sexuality, aggression, the body, constitution.… With respect to clinical technique … new thinking about the principles governing clinical judgment … to address itself to the ways in which the analyst's experience can be brought to bear, both through expression and in restraint, on furthering and deepening the analytic process” (p. 2). Mitchell was already engaged in the thinking-through of Kleinian technique that was to appear as Influence and Autonomy (1997), a work mostly concerned with matters of knowing. These present books, Relationality (2000) and Can Love Last? (2002)—one theoretical and professionally oriented, the other discursive and philosophical and directed to the general reader—are more about feeling and motivation. Together they constitute his last testament and response to his own challenge.

Discussion of Eisold's “Profession of Psychoanalysis”

Arnold Cooper MD

Arnold Cooper

285 Central Park West, Apartment 7S
New York, NY 10024-3006

Arnold Cooper  

KENNETH EISOLD has presented a brilliant description of the rise and decline of the profession of psychoanalysis, a topic of enormous interest now. He offers a sophisticated sociological study of what it is that constitutes a profession, and discusses Freud's tripartite definition of psychoanalysis as an academic discipline, a therapy, and a research method. His aim is (p. 558) “to see more clearly how psychoanalysis has failed—and continues to fail—at establishing itself in the eyes of the public as the profession Freud hoped and believed it had become” He cites a major cause of this failure (p. 560) as psychoanalysts having “borrowed the professional identity of medicine to cover their analytic identities and, in so doing, inadvertently undermined the efforts of psychoanalysis to establish a professional identity in its own right.” Dr. Ei-sold's review of the state of psychoanalysis and his suggested remedies are deeply thoughtful and important. Because I am in agreement with a great deal of what Eisold tells us, I focus on areas that merit further discussion. Following his themes, I focus on the characteristics of a profession, the difficulties confronting us, and possible directions for future solutions.

The term “professional” can be misleading. Part of our confusion may relate to Freud's (1937) famous description of psychoanalysis as one of the “impossible professions.” It is worth examining that quote in detail.

Here let us pause for a moment to assure the analyst that he has our sincere sympathy in the very exacting requirements of his practice. It almost looks as if analysis were the third of those “impossible” professions in which one can be sure only of unsatisfying results. The other two, as has long been agreed, are the bringing-up of children and the government of nations. Obviously we cannot demand that the prospective analyst should be a perfect human being before he takes up analysis, so that only persons of this rare and exalted perfection should enter the profession.

COMPULSIVE SEXUALITY seems to have become a more frequent phenomenon in clinical practices as well as in the general culture, reflected in magazine and newspaper articles, the popular currency of the term “sexual addiction,” and in targeted twelve-step programs. There appears to be one of those confluences of the social and the clinical that are fascinating, one that was clearly emerging even before the Monica Lewinsky-Bill Clinton controversy burst onto the public stage. It seems to me that, as often is the case, old wine has appeared in new bottles. People I understood as showing essentially perverse structures of desire, and as driven in their sexual appetites (sometimes very driven, sometimes less than was claimed) have been calling themselves and diagnosed as “sexual addicts.” Addiction seems to have become—like trauma in recent years—an increasingly popular explanation for troubling goings on.

The thought that joins addiction and trauma may not be entirely random. Both terms locate cause and power outside oneself; a certain passivity and victim status accrues to the afflicted person. The word “addiction,” according to the Oxford English Dictionary, originally meant “a formal giving over or delivery by sentence of court,” from which it came to mean “a surrender, or dedication of any one to a master.” Thus, “addict” is by definition passive; “assigned, made over, bound” are its earliest synonyms. Compare “perversion,” the root meaning of which is “thoroughly turned”—turned from the good, obviously, as its synonyms are “corrupt, incorrect, improper.” Perversion is more active, and the ominous elements are in the person, not in some external master.

THE FIRST HALF of this book looks at eating problems and the clinical demands patients with these difficulties make on their analysts. It shows the ways in which “appetitive desire” (Crastnopol, p. 151) gone wrong creates what can be experienced as unsustainable and uncontain-able hungers that incline individuals to ferociously enact behaviors vis-à-vis food. The individual with an eating problem is attempting to privatize and to solve inside of herself a problematic: How can I manage a need, a desire, an appetite, when need, desire, and appetite have been rendered in me as impermissible, too much or too big?

For the individual with an eating problem, the various negotiations with food—eating, not eating, bingeing, purging, limiting food to certain groups, such as carbohydrates or protein, or avoiding wheat and dairy as a way to control dietary intake—are conceived as solutions to the problem of “appetitive desire.” While their parents, doctors, lovers, friends register their eating behavior as the problem, we are interested in understanding with them why their behaviors appear to them to be a solution to the problem of appetitive desire. We want to enter into the emotional space that allows us and them to see what they are up to when they either refuse to eat when they are hungry, eat more than their bodies can process, or eat only with the intention of ridding themselves of the food. We want them to consider (even if they are initially unable to take the risk) experiencing the sets of feelings and conflicts that eating in accordance with their biological need would engender. We want them to address rather than avoid the psychic difficulties that are encoded in their eating and noneating behaviors.

IN AN EXCELLENT WORK, essential for anyone who supervises, is supervised, or teaches a course on supervision, Frawley-O'Dea and Sarnat suggest a language for thinking about our supervisory relationships, challenge our underlying assumptions, and offer a well-defined structure to this unique analytic relationship.

The book was a gift to me from a former supervisee. Our work had a tenuous beginning. The supervisee was doubtful and wondering if I would be someone available, safe, and authentic enough for her to present her work. But as we submitted to the task of understanding her patients from within our own relational experience, an understanding of the therapeutic and supervisory relationship was enhanced. The book was given to me with the following text underlined:

the supervisory relationship can allow the supervisee to gain a deeper understanding of the treatment method being taught [as they] work together to co-construct, mutually derive, and negotiate meanings that elucidate both the treatment relationship and the supervisory relationship.

By giving attention to the relational projections, transferences, and countertransferences, we traversed the murky relational waters and concluded with an experience that left a profound impact on each of us.

My guess is that others who practice relationally will also recognize their work in the pages of this book.

PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORIES rely on accounts of child development to express their basic assumptions and to buttress their arguments about them. Developmental imagery is a prominent factor in how analysts organize clinical data. Analytic theories establish coherence between their theories of early development, motivation, psychic structure, psychopathology, and clinical technique.

Relational Psychoanalysis and Developmental Thinking: An Overview

Relational psychoanalysis has linked to those developmental models that have seen human contact as primary from the beginning. Within psychoanalysis, British object relationalists, interpersonalists, and self psychologists have highlighted this, while contemporary relationally oriented infant researchers have extended this orientation. They have contradicted the Freudian-Kleinian image of the irrational baby by describing the youngest infants' organizing, interpersonal competences.

Overall, relational analysis provides an acute integration of analytic theory and technique with contemporary developmental psychoanalysis and developmental psychology overall, rooted as it is in the view that people are essentially oriented to human relationships, throughout the life span. But while relational psychoanalysis draws heavily on the infant research image of the adaptive, social infant, it does not subsume its own developmental model to it. While frankly developmentalist, it has synthesized that point of view with a number of other crucial emphases: gender theory, social theory, trauma studies, nonlinear dynamic systems theories, and the irrationalist psychoanalytic orientations, all anchored in a philosophical orientation in contemporary dialectical constructivist hermeneutic epistemologies. In addition, the influence of developmental thinking has been annealed with interpersonal psychoanalysis.

AS WE MOVE DEEPER into the prehistoric caves, the world darkens and looks different. As if from nowhere, suddenly, 13,000-year-old mammoths look down on us with relative disinterest. They stare at the stalactites dripping down like stone icicles beyond us. One stands thoughtful and wooly, his tusks uncomfortably long, never ceasing to grow, wearing down his old age. They call him the patriarch. He is beautifully represented, carved into the stone in different layers of depth, which makes his wooly fur stand out in fuzzy precision. He is carved over scratches made by fingers into stone, scratches similar to ones the cave bear has left behind in the walls to sharpen its claws. The bears were long gone by the time our ancestors entered this cave in Rouffignac, in the Perigord region of what now is France, 13,000 years ago.

I envision our ancestor entering, seeing the carvings left by bear. This must be the way the wall is met, he thinks. So first he makes similar scratches with his fingers, to imitate the ancestor, the bear, who has made his winter beds here for tens of thousands of years. This is the way the ancestor did it, so this is how we begin, honoring our forebears, as a background to our own impressions. Deep inside the earth, carved over a grid of scratches, the patriarch stands looking back toward the mouth of the cave, kilometers away. Four fingers, like a bear's claw, is the matrix. Farther to the right we see two herds of mammoth meeting, looking at each other. The frieze follows the contours of the wall. These are the powers in all their gigantic nature. They meet, face off, maybe peaceably: two tribes of great spirits. This is the largest drawing. It is the cave of the mammoth spirit facing itself—encounter, reflection.

Along the wall I see, shimmying on his belly along the cave barely two feet high, our ancestor on his way to be initiated into the world of the great spirits, the massive mammoth. Facing off with self, meeting self in a great collision or in celebration.

I WAS CONFRONTED with the issue of serious illness several years ago when a lump in my breast was diagnosed as an early stage of breast cancer. I underwent several outpatient procedures during the month after the initial biopsy, which necessitated my canceling and rescheduling sessions with some patients. Treatment for the cancer included chemotherapy and radiation, administered over a course of approximately eight months. My appearance changed; I lost my hair as a result of the chemotherapy and wore a wig.

A personal crisis causes a disruption to the state of ongoing regularity and relative predictability of one's life. It is a time of acute emotional disequilibrium in which the boundaries that people set up to protect themselves are bombarded by the presence of immediate situational stress. Psychoanalysts must contend not only with the explosion of the regularity and dependability of their personal life caused by the crisis, but also with the anxiety of disruption to their patients. The crisis fires questions that need to be immediately answered. Will patients' sessions need to be canceled? How will the cancellations be explained? What, if anything, should patients be told about the reasons behind the disruption to the predictability of their scheduled appointments?

ONE cannot help being profoundly moved by Nina Farhi's case presentation. The reader becomes almost as captivated by the narrative as was Ms. Farhi by her analysand. It was an extraordinary clinical involvement, and the author clearly shows how she had been affected by it and reflected long and hard about what had transpired—in the silences and in the nether world beneath the sound of words. Whatever the psychoanalytic orientation of the reader, he or she will unanimously agree that a profound, poignant, and exquisite psychoanalytic happening had taken place.

The Case Presentation

Briefly in summary, Anne, the analysand, who was a single female in her mid-thirties and ungainly tall, presents herself imposingly for analysis to Ms. Farhi, who acknowledges that she went into a virtual submissive trance, feeling that the analysand-to-be presented her with a fait accompli for her to become her analyst. The analysand had no memory of her past.1 The name she proffered to Ms. Farhi was that of her mother, both first name and last (thus the title of the presentation), a practice that she initiated when mother and father divorced.

The past history is horrendous. Her mother had to undergo a hysterectomy along with the delivery of her daughter and quickly afterward fell ill with a severe postpartum depression. The analysand was nursed and reared by a succession of nannies and never really experienced true mothering by her mother.

1The childhood amnesia in this case reminds one of Mary Main's Adult Attachment Interview in which the way that an adult narrates his or her childhood history becomes a marker for the quality and typology of attachment (Main, Kaplan & Cassidy, 1985; Grice, 1989).99

FOR FREUD in 1937, psychoanalysis may have been one of the “impossible professions,” along with teaching and politics, but it had unquestionably taken its place among the privileged occupations of the modern world. It was a profession.

Earlier, in 1916, it had been a “movement,” earlier still a “cause.” But gradually over the years it seemed to achieve the status for which it had slowly and inexorably striven. That is, like other professions, it possessed an esoteric and specialized body of knowledge, which it sought to develop and extend through journals, books, and conferences; it established institutes to train practitioners in the skillful use of that knowledge; it monitored standards of competence through professional associations; and it developed standards of ethical practice. As a result, psychoanalysts were coming to have a certain recognizable social identity and, like other professionals, lay claim to a corresponding social status.

The professionalization of psychoanalysis in this period paralleled the development of other professions out of relatively unorganized, unregulated, and vulnerable vocations. Social theorists in the earlier part of the century, such as Weber and Durkheim, essentially agreed with the profession's own self-assessment as self-regulating and stable occupations occupying a unique, privileged social position. For them, the idealized position of the professions stemmed in large part from the idea that professions took responsibility for their own development and practice, providing an alternative to the unbridled competition of the marketplace. No doubt, it was this idealized concept of the professions that Freud had in mind when he staked the claim of psychoanalysis.

But recent sociology of the professions questions this claim, calling attention to the “project” of professionalization, the process by means of which a practice or vocation acquires and sustains the status of a profession. IT WAS a beautiful Friday in autumn, the kind of day that reminds me why I live in Vermont. I was feeling jubilant that my internal medicine patients were all taken care of for the weekend, I was not on call, and I was anticipating with pleasure my upcoming session with Mr. A. He was my first analytic patient, and thus far the work with him had been going quite well; we had quickly established a good therapeutic alliance, he was committed to the process, and was working hard in his analysis. I felt confident that my plan to change careers from medicine to psychoanalysis was not only right, but indeed inspired.

Mr. A's sessions characteristically began with a litany of details, in keeping with his rather obsessive nature. At the beginning of his analysis, approximately one year prior to this session, it often took him the first thirty minutes of the hour to feel comfortable enough to abandon his scripted text. By the time of the session reported here, though, he usually settled in after about ten minutes. This particular hour began quite differently, however, with him asking if he could sit on the footstool next to my feet. In answer to my inquiry, he explained that he felt particularly emotionally close to me that day, and needed the physical proximity. I wondered what to do.

Looking back on my medical career, I think it is fair to say that I attempted to be the “good object” for all of my patients, whether tending to them during catastrophic illness or simply providing routine health maintenance. I felt able to provide unfailing care for even the most “difficult” of patients, and often accepted referrals of such patients from other physicians in the community. In an environment of unquestioning provision of care, all interpersonal negotiations between patient and physician are geared toward that care, and the subjectivity of the physician is considered relevant only to the extent that it serves that purpose.

NINA FARHI'S compelling and at times harrowing account of her arduous psychoanalytic journey with Anne, and the complex theorizing that frames it, has a great deal to teach us about working with our most disturbing and disturbed patients. It raises a variety of complex questions about the psychoanalytic process itself. These include questions about the surprising, even shocking ways an analytic process takes hold, the role of enactments in both creating and working through impasses, and how patients and analysts forge the most fundamental changes in one another through the creative, largely unconsciously determined challenges and encounters that constitute the fabric of a psychoanalysis. I would like to touch on a few of these issues in the discussion that follows.

As Farhi notes at the outset, it was probably not at all incidental to the process that followed that she was herself a freshly minted psychotherapist when Anne entered her consulting room for the first time. The unconscious determinants of how any given patient selects any given analyst to work with are subtle, profound, and often overlooked, sometimes discerned, if ever, many years into an analysis. The patient's choice of analyst is among the first creative acts of the process, the point at which the patient is choosing and shaping the “medium” in which her analytic work will take place. Would an analytic process have been possible at all with a more seasoned Farhi? IN THE TWELVE YEARS I worked with Anne, she changed her names, both first name and surname variously, six times; she also changed her address seventeen times.

Significantly, as will be seen, on the first occasion she came to see me, she came with her mother's name, and she lived nowhere in particular. She had no friends. And she did not work; she had inherited an income from her grandmother. She spent her time entirely in the company of fellow drug addicts or in the darkness of cinemas.

Looking at the almost giant proportions of the woman who entered my consulting room, now more than twenty years ago, noting her swollen, black, infected fingers, her ankle-length skirt and short, white socks, I felt caught up in a spectacle. She made absolutely no eye contact.

I was struck by her exceptional height—almost two meters—and the poignant babyish self-presentation. The span of her hands, the vast size of her feet seemed somehow dissociated from the rest of her.

I also felt disturbed by her. She seemed blind in her unlooking. As though she were deaf, there was an almost complete lack of resonance in her voice. She did not seem to be nervous of me; indeed, I wondered to what extent she acknowledged me as being there at all.

I experienced no sense of my usual choice as to whether or not I would take her into therapy. She, however, conveyed to me the fact of her arrival and a steely determination that she was there for the duration, no matter how long this would take.

I was immensely struck by the sheer physicality of her presence, or should I also say her nonpresence. There was something compelling in the nonnegotiability of her intention to be in treatment with me that allowed no discussion. It was as if I were to have no personal say in the matter. Her presence was all.

In reality, of course, I did have a choice. I was not yet caught up in her unidimensional world.

75

W.R. BION anticipated our current interest in intersubjectivity, and his object relations theory is specific about key relational phenomena. The cornerstone of his theory of individual and group development is that thinking is a primary emotional need and matures in the context of social communication. He formulated the essential process of how thinking and communicating mutually develop in terms of a model of “container-contained.” The model draws attention to how we hear and think about another's communication, how we convey our experience back, and how this communicative interplay impacts the participants and the immediate future of the relationship.

Bion began formulating these ideas in his work with groups. He discovered that a type of countertransference emerged from taking in the members' projective identifications. Although often painful to absorb and make sense of, the analyst's subjective reactions could be utilized to learn about the group and its members. Bion demonstrated how the clinician, using primary process—the capacity to free-associate, imagine, and dream—and secondary processes, might gather in and decipher the patients' unformulated or unarticulated experience. The analyst's successful subjective transformations, “containing,” of the shared experience, the “contained,” provided the most reliable basis of interpretations.

As he developed his metapsychology, Bion described processes of symbol formation, human development, internal and external object relations, and learning from (and resisting) emotional experience, all illuminated by the notion of container-contained. Additionally, he briefly elaborated three variations: commensal, symbiotic, and parasitic interactions (Bion, 1970, p. 95 see also Billow & Lovett, 1984; Langs, 1978; Symington & Symington, 1996, pp. 56-57).

HARRY STACK SULLIVAN once said that the last thing that happens to you just before you go crazy is that everything becomes clear! Well, I had an epiphany about a year ago, when it occurred to me that the detailed inquiry, particularly the deconstructed detailed inquiry, is really visual, not, as one might reasonably expect, verbal, and that, indeed, the entire psychoanalytic praxis, although annotated in words, actually takes place in a visual-spatial modality. I limn out recent developments in neuroscience that may provide a rationale for this apparent logical inversion. Finally, focusing on visual imagery, I elaborate a primer of psychoanalytic technique that is form—not content—oriented and that I am convinced captures the absolute essence of the psychoanalytic praxis.

It may have been a signal contribution of interpersonal psychoanalysis to posit a disconnect between metapsychology and technique, that is, to suggest that successful therapy may depend more on what one does than what one says about it. I have long claimed that psychoanalysis works as a therapeutic instrument, not because of the correctness of its meta-psycholog(ies), but because of its praxis, that is, what we do when we are plying our trade, rather than how we then proceed to explain what we have done (Levenson, 1972). It seems likely that the inquiry is the therapeutic act; that as Marshall Mcluhan put it, the medium is indeed the message.

BEFORE my candidacy at White I was in treatment with a traditionally trained, highly respected analyst. Looking back I would say that what helped me most was the profound resonance between the courage she openly advocated and the courage of her own actions (inside and outside the treatment). Her resonance made me feel more whole. What I was hearing from her words matched what I was feeling from her actions. She had an integrity that inspired me to strive for something similar.

Resonance transforms. In treatment, supervision, and writing we show people what we think matters, as we talk to them about what matters. If the medium doesn't match the message, if, for example, we preach nonintrusiveness intrusively, our message will transfix more than it will transform. Its recipient will be struck dumb, struggling to make coherent sense out of mystifying discrepancy. Like the parent who advises to “do as I say, not as I do,” the analyst, supervisor, writer who doesn't practice what she preaches is a stultifying, disorienting, and ineffective model.

On the other hand, we are often profoundly affected by encounters with integrity. In his book, Stanley Coen enacts the openness he recommends to his reader.

PSYCHOANALYSIS is currently seeking an expanded theory of interaction. The “relational turn” in psychoanalysis is at the center of current efforts to articulate this expansion (e.g., Aron, 1996; Mitchell, 1993, 1997, 2000; Harris, 1992, 1997; Ghent, 1989, 2002; Benjamin, 1988, 1990, 1995). Within the many streams of thought contributing to this effort, we single out systems views as providing a critical dimension of this expansion. The “dyadic systems view” is our particular contribution to the relational turn in psychoanalysis.

Although systems views have been evident in both psychoanalysis and infant research, each field has come from the opposite bias (Beebe & Lachmann, 1988, 2002). Centrally concerned with interactive regulation in the dyad, infant research on face-to-face interaction has only in the past decade seriously begun addressing self-regulation (Beebe, Jaffe, Chen & Cohen, 2002; Gianinno & Tronick, 1988; Fox, 1994; Thompson, 1994; Tronick, 1989). Similarly, originally centrally occupied with the organization of inner states, psychoanalysis has only in the past decade accorded interaction in the dyad a central place. Mitchell (1993, 1997, 2000) was a key player in this shift within psychoanalysis. We believe, however, that currently there is a discernible theoretical shift away from inner processes toward relational processes, both in relational psychoanalysis and child development research (see Miller, 1996; Overton, 1998; Ghent, 2002), perhaps as a reaction to an historical over-emphasis on inner processes (see Beebe & Lachmann, 1998).

In contrast, in our dyadic systems view, inner and relational processes are co-constructed and equally important (Beebe & Lachmann, 1998). Self-regulation processes and other-regulation processes emerge together

DESPITE the most untimely circumstance that occasioned this volume honoring Stephen Mitchell's contribution to our field, the subject matter itself is a very timely one. Never before in the history of psychoanalysis has it been as possible for practitioners from different theoretical orientations to engage in a respectful, mutually interesting and interested exchange of ideas as at the present moment. For my part, for the better part of the last decade I have been involved in a number of such clinical and theoretical interchanges, and I have also been attempting to gain a greater familiarity with the published work of colleagues whose training and point of view differ markedly from mine. Although I still strongly identify myself as a proponent of modern conflict theory (a direct derivative of traditional Freudian psychoanalysis), I also realize that I have been influenced by my immersion in a study of the thinking of others, including contemporary relational analysts. When one is embarked on such an intellectual journey, it is useful to pause from time to time, to check one's bearings and assess one's present position. I am grateful to the editors for the invitation to participate in this volume, which gives me reason to undertake such a review.

It seems to me that whenever I take a fresh look at my theoretical and clinical stance I come to slightly different conclusions about where I stand, and how I have arrived there. Make no mistake, I shall not claim to have made any radical revision of my thinking, or of my psychoanalytic priorities. The fundamental landscape of my theoretical countryside is unchanged. However, just as the sets of Monet paintings that show the same scene in different conditions of light serve to highlight both the similarities and the differences, I find that the illumination provided by other points of view often show me my familiar surroundings in new and interesting ways.

I think it may prove useful to begin my review with a brief historical note.

Joerg Bose  

KENNETH EISOLD's assessment of the status of our profession is provocative, challenging, and anxiety-inducing, but ultimately optimistic and constructive. True to his basic idea that psychoanalysis is a critical discipline that questions accepted assumptions, Eisold encourages us to be self-critical and to take responsibility for what he sees as the failure of psychoanalysis to remain a respected profession after its initial success with the public. And this is certainly a crucial concern, since the vitality of psychoanalysis and its roots are in the clinical encounter. Eisold thinks of psychoanalysis as having lost authority because it failed to make a move from charismatic authority to technical authority, and presents instead a confused and fragmented picture and cannot demonstrate its effectiveness to a disillusioned public. This is a serious indictment; yet I believe that some of those factors that Eisold sees as liabilities can also paradoxically be seen from another standpoint as essential aspects of psychoanalysis and part of its potential strength as well.

I think it also needs to be noted that in regard to the field's standing with the public there are significant factors outside of the control of the profession that have contributed to the current state of a diminished public interest. Some of the more accessible applied variants of psychoanalysis as well as other forms of psychotherapy have had greater appeal to a public that now can choose from a large variety of treatment alternatives, and practitioners of these alternatives often promise to achieve results in a much shorter time. We also have recently suffered from a rather massive materialistic attack on the mental health field by what the insurance companies have disguised as managed care. This has created striking economic constraints today, in stark contrast to a time when psychoanalysis flourished because insurance coverage was available for long-term mental health treatment. (As a case in point: psychoanalysis was still doing very well in Germany in the 1970s and 1980s when state insurance was paying for long-term psychoanalysis.)

AS A LONGTIME ADMIRER of Dr. Eisold's contributions to the study of psychoanalysis and its organizational infrastructure, I relished the opportunity to again enjoy his nuanced, even-handed observations on our political life. I applaud his courage as well as his scholarship in exploring the secrets, shibboleths, and shameful rigidities of our field. And I welcome his adding his voice to the rising chorus demanding that the psychoanalytic establishment become more attentive to the needs of individuals and society. His discussion of the current beleaguered state of the profession resonates with the concerns finally being acknowledged by organizational leaders, that our field is in serious trouble, and that the trouble is largely of our own making (Lionells, 1999; Prince 1999). Nonetheless, my response to the current essay is difficult to organize. I am not sure I fully understand the premises Dr. Eisold presents concerning the “project” of professionalization, and I find myself unable to fully subscribe to his conclusions because I believe they point in the direction of increasing rather than decreasing the complexity of our situation.

Dr. Eisold introduces a contemporary sociological view of the project of profession building to suggest that psychoanalysis has failed to meet the criteria that ensure being granted exclusive status by the larger community, and therefore has not achieved the stature and prerogatives of other professional groups. He uses these criteria, I think, to explain why psychoanalysis has declined in popularity, attracts fewer patients and students, and has had difficulty withstanding attack by other scientific and professional groups. I confess I am not familiar with this analysis of the “project” of profession building, and cannot speak to the formal aspects of Dr. Eisold's assertions. But I believe that the problems facing psychoanalysis stem as much, or perhaps more, from its historic successes than from whatever its failures in the political and scientific arenas, and I will try to explicate this position.

IN the early 1990s, I participated in a study broadly concerned with the genesis of violent behaviors in a group of hospitalized offenders. Some subjects were in the hospital merely to have a broken wrist set or to investigate a tubercular-sounding cough; others were receiving lengthy psychiatric evaluations following suicide attempts, seizures, unprovoked assaults, or extravagant episodes of mania. The purpose of the research was to employ analytic methodology, in an intensely focused manner, toward the investigation of three conditions that clinical practice, as well as a burgeoning literature, had suggested were correlative to crime: childhood trauma, mental illness, and dissociation. A second, related purpose was to examine the relevancy of dissociation diagnoses to legal issues of competence, consciousness, volition, and sanity.

I interviewed sixty-four men whose crimes ranged from petty larceny to double murder. The vast majority reported having been physically assaulted during childhood. Almost half of those interviewed had endured grisly episodes of maltreatment at the hands of caregivers. Many had suffered severe burns, broken bones, loss of consciousness, ongoing sexual molestation, and threatened—as well as actual—attempts on their lives by parents or parental surrogates.

Considering the sadism of their primary caretakers, it was not surprising to discover that many inmates had well-honed peri- and posttraumatic defense repertoires. When a history of severe maltreatment was coupled with other signs of neurological or psychiatric illness, dissociative tendencies were quite pronounced, and included a frequent and intense resort to derealization, depersonalization, and amnesia.

Of note, the eleven most pathologically dissociative offenders had committed the most vicious crimes: kidnapping, attempted matricide, murder, arson, serial rape, aggravated assault, and armed robbery. Five of these men professed amnesia for their offenses, although none claimed to be innocent of the crimes with which they were charged.

WE ARE SOMETIMES taken prisoner by our metaphors. Their powerful imagery can become so compelling that we forget that they are metaphors and mistake the properties of our metaphorical images for those of the phenomena we are using those images to address. Such, I think, has been the case with the metaphor of depth that has been so central a feature of psychoanalytic discourse. The sheer familiarity of the depth metaphor makes it difficult to recognize the ways in which it has shaped our thinking and obscured or foreclosed other potential ways of understanding the phenomena with which we are confronted in our daily practice. As a consequence, our formulations about personality development, psychopathology, and therapeutic change have been constrained and at times misdirected.

My complaint, it should be clear, is by no means with the use of metaphor per se. As this article itself amply illustrates, my own writing is drenched in metaphor (still another metaphor, of course). Indeed, it is difficult to imagine how psychological inquiry can be pursued in any meaningful manner without extensive use of metaphor. To attempt to do so would lead either to a stultifying impoverishment of thought or to self-deceptions in which metaphor simply goes unnoticed (cf. Lakoff & Johnson, 1980).

Even in the occasional sentence that seems quite devoid of metaphorical imagery, the trace of metaphor can usually be seen if we probe sufficiently, because the very construction of our language depends on metaphor. THIS PAPER is in response to an invited symposium addressing the impact that relational psychoanalysis has had on other psychoanalytic traditions and, specifically with regard to myself, on self psychology. This, of course, is an extremely complex and difficult question—even more so because the development of relational psychoanalysis and the ongoing evolution of self psychology have been occurring on a concurrent time line. While we can focus on the correspondences and differences between relational and contemporary self-psychological theories, influence is probably bi-directional and, therefore, very difficult to assess. Inasmuch as classical self psychology predates relational psychoanalysis, it naturally leads to the reverse question: How did Kohut's self psychology contribute to the development of relational psychoanalysis?

What is “relational psychoanalysis”? Greenberg and Mitchell (1983) first introduced the term to define a fundamental shift that had occurred in the field of psychoanalysis evidenced in the conceptual similarity among a number of contemporary theories that radically departed from the drive/structure model. In contrast to drive/structure models in which drives are central in psychological life, relational theories posit that “relations with others constitute the fundamental building blocks of mental life” (p. 3). Simultaneously and independently, Atwood and Stolorow (1984) introduced their concept of intersubjectivity to designate the inter-subjective fields that are formed by the intersections of two or more subjectivities. Intersubjective and relational fields are equivalent concepts, both capturing the embeddedness of the individual within an intersubjective or relational field (matrix).
